articles.title: The Fish That Opens Its Mouth
articles.dek: On a coral reef, some of the most dangerous fish wait in line to be cleaned by one of the smallest. The apostle John saw that same mix of courage and mercy in the act of confession.
articles.quote: Confession is simply holding still in the light long enough for God to do what he already wanted to do.
articles.illustration: cleaner wrasse coral reef cleaning stations
articles.body:
Drop beneath the surface off Apo Island or Anilao on a bright morning and, if you know where to look, you may find a small spot on the reef where the traffic never seems to stop. A grouper as long as your arm drifts in and hangs motionless in the water. Then it does something that looks almost reckless. It spreads its gill covers wide, opens its mouth, and lets a slender fish no longer than your finger, striped in black and electric blue, swim straight inside.

The little fish is the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, and the spot is what marine biologists call a cleaning station. The wrasse works its way across teeth and gills, picking off parasites, dead skin, and bits of infection the larger fish could never reach on its own. Researchers on the Great Barrier Reef have watched a single cleaner inspect more than two thousand visitors in one day. Many of those visitors signal that they want help by holding a special pose, head tilted and fins spread, and some even shift their color while they wait. Predators that would swallow a fish that size anywhere else let it come and go unharmed. When scientists removed cleaner wrasses from patches of reef, the fish living there grew fewer and less healthy over the following months. The healing on that reef belongs to the fish willing to come into the open, hold still, and be seen.

Somewhere in the city of Ephesus, near the end of the first century, an old man was trying to explain that same mystery to a frightened church. Early Christian tradition remembers him as John, the last of the twelve apostles still living. His congregations had just been through a painful split. A group of teachers had walked out, taking friends and families with them, and John would later write of them, "They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us" (1 John 2:19). These teachers seem to have claimed a higher spiritual knowledge that lifted them above ordinary moral struggle. Sin, in their view, was something the truly enlightened had outgrown. The believers left behind, people who still lost their tempers and still lay awake ashamed, must have wondered whether they were the ones who had missed something.

John answers them by starting with his own hands. He writes about the One "which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked at and our hands have touched" (1 John 1:1). The Greek word for touched, psēlaphaō, describes feeling something physically, the way a person reaches through the dark for a wall. This was the disciple who had leaned against Jesus at the Last Supper (John 13:23–25). Whatever the new teachers offered, John had something firmer: he had stood close enough to the Light to feel His breathing.

From there he lays down the foundation of everything that follows: "God is light; in him there is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). Then, one claim at a time, he takes apart the boasts of the departed teachers. Anyone who claims fellowship with God while living in darkness, he says, is lying (1:6). Anyone who claims to be without sin is self-deceived (1:8), and anyone who insists they have never sinned at all "make[s] him out to be a liar" (1:10). Between those warnings, like a doorway in a stone wall, John sets one sentence of pure invitation.

"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:9)

The word John uses for confess is homologeō, built from two smaller Greek words that mean "same" and "to speak." To confess is to say the same thing God says about what has happened. God already sees the bitterness, the lie told to the boss, the habit hidden on the phone. Confession adds nothing to His knowledge. It is the moment we stop arguing with what He sees and finally agree with Him out loud. Like the grouper on the reef, we hold the posture that says, "Here it is. I cannot reach this by myself."

What follows is the line that surprises careful readers. John says God is "faithful and just" to forgive. We would expect the word merciful, because mercy is what a guilty person hopes for. Justice sounds like the very thing a sinner should fear. John explains himself a few lines later: "We have an advocate with the Father," he writes, naming Him as "Jesus Christ, the Righteous One" (1 John 2:1), and "He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world" (2:2). The word for advocate, paraklētos, was used for someone called to stand beside you in court, a defender who speaks on your behalf. One way to read John's logic is this: because Jesus has already paid the debt in full, God's own justice now stands on the side of the person who confesses. Forgiving that person is simply God keeping His word and honoring a payment already made.

King David learned this long before John put it into words. "When I kept silent," he wrote, "my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long" (Psalm 32:3). Then everything changed: "I acknowledged my sin to you and did not cover up my iniquity... And you forgave the guilt of my sin" (Psalm 32:5). The silence was what had been hurting him, and the confession was what began the healing.

There is also quiet comfort in the tense of John's verbs. When he writes that the blood of Jesus "purifies us from all sin" (1 John 1:7), the Greek describes something ongoing, a cleansing that keeps happening as we keep walking in the light. The cleaning station on the reef stays open all day, and fish return to it again and again because parasites keep coming back. In the same way, walking in the light describes a lifelong habit of returning to God, honest and open, as often as we need to.

Many of us were raised to handle our failures privately. We keep face, we avoid hiya, and we try to fix things quietly before anyone notices, sometimes even before God notices, as if that were possible. John gently offers another way. Tonight, before you sleep, you might name one specific thing to God in plain words, the actual words He would use, and then thank Him that He is faithful and just to forgive it. If a particular sin has held you for years, consider telling one trusted, mature believer, since Scripture says, "Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). Light shared with a faithful friend often loosens what years of private effort could not.

It matters, too, how John addresses his readers as he finishes this thought. He calls them "My dear children" (1 John 2:1), using the Greek teknia, a tender word for little ones. He writes so that they will not sin, and in the very same breath he reassures them about what happens when they do. An old man who had touched the Light wanted wounded, struggling believers to know that the way back was wide open.

The grouper on the reef has no idea how brave it looks, opening its mouth to something small enough to swallow. It only knows that the itching stops when it comes into the open. Confession is simply holding still in the light long enough for God to do what he already wanted to do. Whatever you have been carrying in the dark, the Advocate is already standing beside you, and the One who sees it all is waiting, faithful and just, to make you clean.

articles.title: Where the River Goes
articles.dek: In Ezekiel's vision, a thin trickle under a temple door becomes a river deep enough to heal the Dead Sea. God's life still starts small, and it still runs toward the places that feel past saving.
articles.quote: The trickle God gives you is enough to begin, and it grows deeper every time you let it run downhill toward someone who is dry.
articles.body:
In 1976 an economics professor named Muhammad Yunus walked out of Chittagong University and into Jobra, a village a short distance from campus, looking for answers his textbooks had not given him. Bangladesh had just come through a terrible famine, and the theories he taught in his lecture hall seemed to have nothing to say to the hungry families living near the university. In Jobra he met a young woman named Sufiya Begum, who wove beautiful bamboo stools. She had no money to buy bamboo, so she borrowed from a trader, who then made her sell the finished stools back to him at whatever price he named. After a full day of skilled work she kept a profit of about two cents.

Yunus asked his students to list everyone in the village caught in the same kind of arrangement. They found forty-two names. The total those forty-two families owed, the sum that kept them bound to the moneylenders, came to about twenty-seven US dollars. Yunus took the money out of his own pocket and lent it to them, asking only that they pay him back when they could, and they did. That small loan became the seed of Grameen Bank, which went on to lend to millions of the world's poorest borrowers, most of them women, and in 2006 Yunus and the bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize. The idea travelled a long way. In San Pablo, Laguna, the group now known as CARD adapted it for Filipino mothers running sari-sari stores and small farms.

What moves me most is how small the beginning was. Twenty-seven dollars would barely pay for a family dinner in many cities today. Still, it went straight to the place where it was needed most, the poorest corner of a struggling village, and once it got there it kept widening. The prophet Ezekiel saw something very much like this, though in his vision the thing that grew was a river.

Ezekiel was a priest who never served in the temple he had trained for. He was taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC, and about eleven years later the Babylonians burned Jerusalem and its temple to the ground. Before that disaster, Ezekiel had watched in a vision as the glory of the Lord rose and left the temple (Ezekiel 10:18–19). So by the twenty-fifth year of the exile (Ezekiel 40:1) his people had no temple, no king and no land. That was when God gave him a long, careful vision of a restored temple, measured down to the cubit, and in chapter 43 the glory finally came home. Chapter 47 is where all of it leads.

An angelic guide brings Ezekiel back to the temple entrance, and he sees "water coming out from under the threshold of the temple toward the east" (Ezekiel 47:1). It is a very small flow. The NIV says the water "was trickling from the south side" (Ezekiel 47:2). The Hebrew word, mepakkim, appears nowhere else in the Old Testament, and many scholars link it to pak, the word for a small flask or vial of oil (1 Samuel 10:1). It suggests water dribbling out the way oil drips from the mouth of a little jar. The healing of the land begins as a thin line of water you could stop with one finger.

Then the guide starts walking east with a measuring line. After a thousand cubits, roughly half a kilometer, he leads Ezekiel through water that is "ankle-deep." Another thousand, and it is "knee-deep." Another thousand, and it is "up to the waist" (Ezekiel 47:3–4). At the next measurement it has become "a river that I could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough to swim in" (Ezekiel 47:5). The guide turns to him and asks, "Son of man, do you see this?" (Ezekiel 47:6). When they climb back onto the bank, the dry slopes are suddenly lined with trees.

Then the guide explains where the river is going. It runs down into the Arabah, the deep rift valley, and empties into the Dead Sea, which the Hebrew Bible usually calls the Salt Sea. Ezekiel's first readers knew that place well. It lies about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest land on earth, and its water is close to ten times saltier than the ocean. No fish live in it. The guide promises this:

"Swarms of living creatures will live wherever the river flows. There will be large numbers of fish, because this water flows there and makes the salt water fresh; so where the river flows everything will live." (Ezekiel 47:9)

He adds that fishermen will stand along the shore, "from En Gedi to En Eglaim," spreading their nets (Ezekiel 47:10). En Gedi was a real spring-fed oasis on the western edge of that bitter lake, so the picture is a familiar desert shore crowded with fishing boats. Along both banks, fruit trees bear a new crop every month, "because the water from the sanctuary flows to them," and "their leaves" serve "for healing" (Ezekiel 47:12).

Real rivers get bigger as other streams pour into them. Ezekiel's river gets deeper with every thousand cubits, and the vision never mentions a single tributary joining it. The only explanation the text gives is the source. All of its depth comes from the house where God has come back to live, which is why the city in the vision's last verse carries the name "THE LORD IS THERE" (Ezekiel 48:35). One way to read this is that God's life gains strength as it travels away from the sanctuary and out into the world. That is the reverse of how we usually think. We tend to assume holiness stays strongest close to the altar and grows thin and diluted out among ordinary, damaged people. In Ezekiel's vision, the water is strongest when it reaches the Dead Sea.

The river also flows downhill. It heads for the lowest, saltiest, most hopeless place in the region, as though that were where it had wanted to go all along. The rest of Scripture keeps this picture. Jesus stood up at a feast in Jerusalem and said, "Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within them" (John 7:38). The Bible closes with the same river, "flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb," lined with trees whose leaves "are for the healing of the nations" (Revelation 22:1–2). The river that started under a temple door now flows through people.

That makes the vision very personal. Most of us have a Dead Sea somewhere in our relationships: a sibling we have not spoken to since the argument over Lola's house, a coworker everyone has quietly given up on, a friendship that went salty years ago. These places feel too far gone for anything we could offer. What we have usually feels like a trickle, a few words of apology, an hour of listening, a little patience we are not sure will last. Yunus faced forty-two families trapped in debt with twenty-seven dollars, and it was enough to begin, because he carried it to the people who needed it.

Ezekiel's river makes the same promise. The trickle God gives you is enough to begin, and it grows deeper every time you let it run downhill toward someone who is dry. You do not have to fill the river yourself, because its depth comes from the God whose name is "THE LORD IS THERE." What you can do is choose one person in your own Dead Sea and send them something small this week, a message, a visit or a kept promise. Then trust the One who asked Ezekiel, "Do you see this?" to show you, a thousand cubits at a time, how far that small flow can go.

articles.title: The Furrows on Your Back
articles.dek: Psalm 129 remembers years of hurt without flinching, then ends with a farmer's image: a plowed field is a field being made ready for harvest.
articles.quote: God cuts the cords that pull the plow, and then he plants in the furrows it left behind.
articles.body:
On July 12, 2013, a girl turned sixteen at a podium in the United Nations in New York. Nine months earlier, a gunman had stopped her school bus in Pakistan's Swat Valley, asked which of the girls was Malala, and shot her in the head. She was flown to Birmingham, England, where surgeons rebuilt part of her skull and she slowly learned to walk and speak with ease again. Now she stood in front of hundreds of young people from around the world, and her voice was steady.

"The terrorists thought that they would change my aims and stop my ambitions," she said, "but nothing changed in my life except this: weakness, fear and hopelessness died. Strength, power and courage was born." The hall rose to its feet. What moved people most that day was simply the fact that she was standing there. The attack had been real, and its marks were still on her body, and yet the girl someone had tried to silence was speaking to the whole world on her birthday.

An old Hebrew song carries that same sound, and it was written for ordinary people to sing together. Psalm 129 belongs to the fifteen Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134), which pilgrims sang as they walked uphill toward Jerusalem for the great festivals. Picture families on dusty roads, whole villages joining the march, with a song leader calling out a line and the crowd echoing it back. In this psalm the leader even tells them when to answer: "'They have greatly oppressed me from my youth,' let Israel say" (Psalm 129:1).

"From my youth" reaches all the way back to the nation's childhood, to brick kilns in Egypt and taskmasters with whips. After that came raiders, empires, sieges and exile, generation after generation. The pilgrims sang the line once, and then they sang it again, because some pain deserves to be said twice. On the second time, though, they added a few words that changed the whole song: "they have greatly oppressed me from my youth, but they have not gained the victory over me" (Psalm 129:2). The Hebrew is short and blunt, lo yakhlu li, which means something like "they were not able against me." The enemies had plenty of strength. What they lacked was the power to finish the job.

Then the singer reaches for a picture every farmer in the crowd would understand: "Plowmen have plowed my back and made their furrows long" (Psalm 129:3). An ancient plow was a wooden beam with a sharpened point, dragged through the soil by oxen bound to it with ropes. The image is of a back so beaten that the welts run across it like rows in a field. Isaiah uses a similar picture when he describes Israel's suffering, saying the oppressors made her "back like the ground" (Isaiah 51:23). This is honest language about real wounds, and the psalm lets the worshiper say it out loud in the middle of a festival crowd.

"But the LORD is righteous; he has cut me free from the cords of the wicked." (Psalm 129:4)

The word translated "cords" is avot, the thick ropes used in harnessing. In the flow of the picture, one way to read this verse is that God walks into the field and cuts the ropes that bind the oxen to the plow. He does not have to argue with every plowman or wrestle every animal. He severs the harness, and the whole operation stops halfway down the row. The beam drops into the dirt, the oxen wander off, and the plowing that seemed endless simply ends. The verb, qitstsets, carries the sense of cutting something into pieces, so the cords are finished for good.

The second half of the psalm turns to those who did the plowing, and its imagery stays on the farm. The singer prays that they will "be like grass on the roof, which withers before it can grow; a reaper cannot fill his hands with it, nor one who gathers fill his arms" (Psalm 129:6–7). Houses in ancient Israel had flat roofs of packed earth, and after a rain, stray seeds blown up there would sprout green almost overnight. Within a day or two of sun they were brown and gone, because there was no depth of soil beneath them. No harvester ever bothered to climb up with a sickle.

Then comes the last line, which quotes the greeting people called out across the fields at harvest time: "The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD" (Psalm 129:8). We hear this very exchange in the book of Ruth, when Boaz arrives at his barley field and says to the workers, "The LORD be with you!" and they answer, "The LORD bless you!" (Ruth 2:4). The psalm prays that the oppressors will never hear that greeting, because nothing they grow will ever be worth gathering. These closing verses can sound harsh to us, yet they are a prayer that hands justice over to God instead of taking it into one's own hands.

Put the two halves side by side and a quiet surprise appears. The people who held the plow end up as thin grass on a rooftop, with no soil, no roots and no harvest. The one whose back was plowed is left with long, deep furrows, and every farmer singing on that road knew what furrows are for. A field is plowed right before it is sown. The psalm never says this outright, but it seems to leave the thought hanging in the air for the listener to finish. The prophet Hosea uses the same farming language when he urges God's people to "break up your unplowed ground" so they can "reap the fruit of unfailing love" (Hosea 10:12). God cuts the cords that pull the plow, and then he plants in the furrows it left behind.

Many of us carry furrows of our own. Some were dug by a parent's harsh words that still echo decades later, and others by years of working abroad, far from children who grew up over video calls. Some came from a business that collapsed, an illness that changed the shape of a family, or a betrayal by someone at church. Psalm 129 never asks us to pretend these marks are not there. It gives us permission to say "they have greatly oppressed me" twice, with feeling, in front of God and in front of the people walking beside us.

Then it teaches us the second sentence. Whatever has pressed on you from your youth has had its strength, but it has not had the last word, because the Lord is righteous and he knows how to cut a harness. The apostle Paul, who carried real scars from real whips, put it this way: "We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed" (2 Corinthians 4:8–9). The places where life dug deepest into him became the very places where his compassion and his letters grew.

Before the day is over, you might try praying this psalm in your own words, the way the pilgrims sang it. Name honestly the thing that has plowed across your life, say it twice if you need to, and then add the line that belongs to every child of God: "but it has not gained the victory over me." After that, borrow the harvest greeting and give it away to someone who is still standing in a hard field, perhaps in a text message or a word at the door: "The blessing of the LORD be on you."

A young woman stood at a podium with scars that would never fully fade, and the world heard courage instead of defeat. Your furrows may still be visible too, and that is no shame at all. The plow has been cut loose, the field belongs to the Lord, and the deep rows in your story may be exactly where he intends to grow something worth gathering.

articles.title: The Cells That Know When to Stand Down
articles.dek: Proverbs puts two opposite commands side by side about answering a fool. A Nobel-winning discovery about the immune system shows why both of them are wise.
articles.quote: Love decides whether to speak or to stay silent, and either way it is aiming at the other person's healing.
articles.body:
In the early 1980s, a young Japanese researcher named Shimon Sakaguchi was chasing an idea most of his field had decided to give up on. Immunologists had once suspected that the body kept a special class of cells whose job was to calm the immune system down, but the early evidence had been messy, and by the middle of that decade the phrase "suppressor cells" had become something researchers avoided saying out loud. Funding grew thin and many colleagues moved on to other questions. Sakaguchi kept working, first in Japan and later in the United States, because he was convinced the body must have some way of telling its own soldiers when to hold their fire.

In 1995 he showed that he was right. He identified a small population of what are now called regulatory T cells, white blood cells that move through the body restraining the immune system from attacking healthy tissue. A few years later, Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, studying a strain of mice that suffered severe autoimmune disease, traced the problem to a single gene, later named Foxp3, and Sakaguchi soon connected that gene to the very cells he had found. In October 2025 the three shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Their work explains something every doctor and nurse sees on the ward: an immune system that never engages lets infection run wild, and an immune system that never stands down turns on the body it was meant to protect. Health depends on knowing, moment by moment, which response the situation calls for.

Long before anyone had a microscope, the book of Proverbs understood the same principle about the human tongue. It put it in a way so blunt that it has puzzled readers for centuries.

The chapter comes from a collection that Proverbs 25:1 tells us was "compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah," royal scribes around 700 BC who gathered and arranged Solomon's sayings. When they reached what we call chapter 26, they placed together a cluster of twelve verses, nearly every one of them about the fool. The Hebrew word here is kesil, and it does not describe someone with low intelligence. The kesil is a person who has closed his mind, who is confident, loud, and uninterested in being corrected. Proverbs 18:2 sketches him perfectly: "Fools find no pleasure in understanding but delight in airing their own opinions."

The portraits in Proverbs 26:1–6 are vivid and a little humorous. "Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, honor is not fitting for a fool" (Prov 26:1). In ancient Israel the wheat harvest came in the dry season, so rain at harvest was so unusual that in 1 Samuel 12:17–18 the prophet Samuel called for thunder and rain at that time as a sign from God. Giving a fool honor is that out of place. A few verses later the scribes add, "Sending a message by the hands of a fool is like cutting off one's feet or drinking poison" (Prov 26:6). Anyone who has trusted an important errand to the wrong person knows exactly what that feels like.

Then, in the middle of these images, the editors set two sayings back to back that seem to cancel each other out:

"Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be just like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes." (Proverbs 26:4–5)

Ancient readers saw the tension immediately. The Talmud records that some of the rabbis once considered withdrawing Proverbs from public use because these verses appeared to contradict each other (Shabbat 30b). Their eventual answer was that the two sayings apply to different situations, and that is the heart of it. The scribes who placed these lines together were too careful to have missed the clash. One good way to read the pairing is that they set the two commands side by side on purpose, so that the reader could never turn wisdom into a single rule to follow without thinking.

Each verse names its own danger. Verse 4 warns about what happens to you: if you meet a fool on his terms, matching his insults and his heat, you will become just like him. Verse 5 warns about what happens to him and to everyone listening: if foolishness goes unanswered, the fool grows more certain he is right, and others may believe him. The phrase "according to his folly" seems to carry two shades of meaning. In the first verse it means using his methods, while in the second it means answering in a way that fits his folly and exposes it. Proverbs asks you to hold both dangers in mind and to ask God which one is greater in this particular moment. That is exactly what a regulatory T cell does in the body, and exactly what Paul prayed for the church in Colossians 4:6: "Let your conversation be always full of grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone."

Jesus lived both verses perfectly. When the Pharisees tried to trap Him with a question about paying taxes to Caesar, He answered, and His answer exposed the trap and sent them away amazed: "So give back to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's" (Matt 22:21). Yet when Herod, who only wanted entertainment, questioned Him before the crucifixion, Luke records that Herod "plied him with many questions, but Jesus gave him no answer" (Luke 23:9). The same Lord chose to speak in one room and to keep silent in another, and in both He was entirely wise and entirely loving.

There is good news buried in this passage, too, and it reaches past our arguments to our own hearts. If we are honest, each of us has been the kesil at some point, sure of ourselves and deaf to God. The Lord could have answered us strictly according to our folly. Instead, Psalm 103:10 tells us, "he does not treat us as our sins deserve or repay us according to our iniquities." At the cross God did both things Proverbs describes. He refused to become like us in our sin, and He exposed our pride so completely that no one can stay wise in his own eyes before it. Paul says the message of the cross looks like foolishness to the world, "for the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom" (1 Cor 1:25). God's answer to fools like us was His Son, given in love, "while we were still sinners" (Rom 5:8).

That changes the way we handle the fools in our own lives. Most Filipinos know the moment well: a tito forwards an outrageous post into the family group chat, or a coworker baits you in front of the whole office, and your thumbs are already moving. Before you reply, you can take a breath and ask the two questions this passage hands you. Will answering pull me into his tone until I sound just like him? Will staying silent leave him, or someone younger who is reading along, believing something false and harmful? Sometimes the wisest answer is a gentle private message instead of a public reply, offered "with gentleness and respect," as Peter puts it (1 Pet 3:15). Sometimes it is a kind silence and a prayer for that person. Love decides whether to speak or to stay silent, and either way it is aiming at the other person's healing.

Sakaguchi spent years trusting that the body had been designed with wisdom in it, and he was right. You can trust that God has also given you His Spirit to guide your words, one conversation at a time. The next time a foolish word comes your way today, pause long enough to ask Him which danger is greater. He answered your folly with grace, and He will gladly teach you to answer others the same way.
